e.etymology: From Latin Patricius (patrician, of noble rank), the name of the fifth-century missionary who became the patron saint of Ireland.
namesakes: Patrick Stewart (actor, Star Trek and X-Men)

assoc.t: Saint Patrick, patron saint of Ireland
Patrick Star, SpongeBob's starfish best friend

e.etymology: Matches Greek Kyrie (O Lord), familiar from the prayer Kyrie eleison. As a boys' name it rose in the United States with basketball star Kyrie Irving.

assoc.t: Kyrie Irving, NBA star
Kyrie eleison, the Lord have mercy prayer
Kyrie, 1985 hit song by Mr. Mister

e.etymology: A short form of Nicholas and its relatives (Nicola, Nicolas, Nikolaus), from Greek nike (victory) plus laos (people). It has been a given name in its own right since the 20th century.
namesakes: Nico (German singer with the Velvet Underground)
Nico di Angelo (character in the Percy Jackson books)

assoc.t: Nico, singer with the Velvet Underground

e.etymology: From the English bird name, Middle English wrenne. It began as a nickname and surname and is a recent choice as a first name, mostly for girls.

assoc.t: wren, a small brown songbird
Christopher Wren, architect of St Paul's Cathedral

e.etymology: From Griffinus, a Latinized form of the Welsh name Gruffudd (Griffith), borne by medieval Welsh kings; its second element means lord. It matches the name of the mythical beast.
namesakes: Peter Griffin (the father in Family Guy)

assoc.t: griffin, mythical beast that is half lion, half eagle
the Griffin family of Family Guy

e.etymology: From a Frankish name built on Germanic rik (ruler, king) plus hard (brave, strong). The Normans brought it to England, where three kings bore it.
namesakes: Richard the Lionheart (crusader king of England)
e.note: The traditional nickname Dick is also vulgar slang, so most Richards now go by Rick, Rich or Richie.

e.meaning: form of Elijah, my God is Yahweh; in Welsh, benevolent
e.etymology: From a surname with two sources: Middle English Elis, a form of Elias (Elijah), and the Welsh name Elisedd, from elus (kind, benevolent).

assoc.t: Ellis Island, historic immigration station in New York

e.meaning: home ruler, by way of Harriet
e.etymology: A pet form of Harriet, the English form of French Henriette, feminine of Henry (home ruler). The l for r swap is the same one that made Molly from Mary.
namesakes: Hallie Parker (one of the twins in The Parent Trap)

assoc.t: Halley's Comet, by sound

e.etymology: The Italian form of Ariadne, the Cretan princess of Greek myth who helped Theseus escape the labyrinth. Ariadne is usually read as most holy.

assoc.t: Ariana Grande, pop star, who spells it with one n

e.meaning: uncertain; often given as white hawk
e.etymology: A medieval form of Gawain, the Arthurian knight, first recorded as Old French Gauvain. The form Gavin survived in Scotland and spread through the English-speaking world from the 1960s.
namesakes: Gavin Rossdale (singer of the band Bush)

e.etymology: Coined toward the end of the 20th century, as a combination of Kay and Lee or as a form of the surnames Cayley and Keeley.
From Italian Gemma, Latin gemma (jewel, also bud). A medieval Italian name, borne by Dante's wife, and a favorite in Britain in the 1980s.
From the fragrant flower, whose name came through French and Arabic from Persian yasamin. Disney's Aladdin (1992) lifted it to its American peak.

assoc.t: Princess Jasmine of Disney's Aladdin
jasmine, the fragrant flower, tea and rice

e.etymology: From a Scottish clan name and English surname that began as a nickname for a big man, Anglo-Norman graunt, from Latin grandis (large).
namesakes: Ulysses S. Grant (Civil War general and eighteenth president)

assoc.t: Ulysses S. Grant, Civil War general and president
grant, money awarded for research or study
a Grant, slang for a fifty-dollar bill

e.etymology: The Latin and most common international spelling of Sarah, from Hebrew Sarah (princess, noblewoman), the wife of Abraham in Genesis.

assoc.t: Sara Lee breads, frozen desserts and deli meats
Sara, 1979 Fleetwood Mac song

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname for a tailor, from Old French tailleur (cutter). It became a first name for boys and then girls in the United States in the 1980s and 1990s.

assoc.t: Taylor Swift, pop superstar
Taylor acoustic guitars

e.etymology: A short form of Germanic names beginning with adal (noble), such as Adelaide. It is also a Latinized form of the biblical Hebrew name Adah (adornment).
namesakes: Ada Lovelace (19th-century mathematician, first computer programmer)

assoc.t: Ada Lovelace, pioneer of computer programming
ADA, the Americans with Disabilities Act

e.etymology: From the aspen, the quaking poplar of the Rocky Mountains, and from the Colorado ski town named for the trees. A modern American nature name.

assoc.t: Aspen, Colorado ski resort town
aspen, the quaking tree of the Rockies

e.meaning: possibly boomerang, from an Aboriginal Australian word
e.etymology: An Australian name of uncertain origin, possibly from kylie, a Noongar word for a boomerang. It is unrelated to Kyle. Singer Kylie Minogue carried it around the English-speaking world.
namesakes: Kylie Jenner (reality star and cosmetics mogul)

assoc.t: Kylie Jenner, reality star and cosmetics mogul
Kylie Minogue, Australian pop star
Kylie Cosmetics, Kylie Jenner's makeup line

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Raphael, from Hebrew Rafa'el (God has healed), the archangel of healing.

assoc.t: Raphael, red-masked Ninja Turtle, spelled with ph

e.etymology: From Greek Phoibe, feminine of phoibos (bright), a Titan linked with the moon and an epithet of Artemis. A Phoebe also appears in Paul's letter to the Romans.
namesakes: Phoebe Buffay (the quirky friend on Friends)
Phoebe Waller-Bridge (creator and star of Fleabag)

assoc.t: Phoebe Buffay, the quirky one on Friends
phoebe, a small North American flycatcher

e.etymology: A modern American form of Adeline with the -lyn ending, also read as Ada plus Lyn. Adeline goes back to Germanic adal (noble).
The Tongan and Fijian form of Malachi, from Hebrew Mal'akhi (my messenger), the last of the Old Testament prophets. In the US it also serves as a phonetic spelling of Malachi.
From Hebrew ari (lion), a short form of Aryeh. It is also an Old Norse name meaning eagle, and a pet form of Ariel, Ariana and Ariella.

assoc.t: Ari, fan nickname for Ariana Grande

e.etymology: From Greek euangelion (good news, gospel). Henry Wadsworth Longfellow introduced it in his 1847 poem Evangeline, about Acadian lovers separated by exile.

assoc.t: Evangeline, Longfellow's 1847 epic poem
Evangeline, the star in Disney's Princess and the Frog

e.etymology: A modern name read either as a spelling of Mila, the Slavic pet form of names with mil (gracious, dear), or as a feminine form of Miles and Milo.
From Moll, a medieval English pet form of Mary in which l replaced r, plus -y. It has been an independent name for centuries and is strongly associated with Ireland.
namesakes: Molly Weasley (the Weasley mother in Harry Potter)

assoc.t: molly, slang for the party drug MDMA
Molly McIntire, American Girl doll

e.note: Molly is also common slang for the drug MDMA (ecstasy).

e.etymology: From Old Norse Eiríkr, most likely ei (ever, always) plus ríkr (ruler). Danish settlers brought it to England, and it was revived in the 19th century.

assoc.t: Prince Eric of Disney's The Little Mermaid
Eric Cartman of South Park

e.meaning: sea, from Hawaiian kai; also a Nordic pet form of Katarina
e.etymology: In Scandinavia and Estonia Kaia is a short form of Katarina (Catherine). In the United States it is more often taken as a feminine form of Kai, Hawaiian for sea.
namesakes: Kaia Gerber (model, daughter of Cindy Crawford)

e.meaning: night, as a form of Leila; also short for Delilah
e.etymology: A spelling of Lila, which is both a variant of the Arabic name Leila (night) and a short form of the biblical Hebrew name Delilah.
From an English surname, usually a variant of Priestley: Old English preost (priest) plus leah (wood, clearing). As a first name it nods to Elvis Presley.

assoc.t: Elvis Presley, the King of Rock and Roll

e.etymology: Used in Spanish as Elián and often treated as a relative of Elias (Elijah). Americans know it from Elián González, the Cuban boy at the center of a 2000 custody dispute.

assoc.t: Elián González, Cuban boy in a 2000 custody dispute
